identityLeakageWarning: Packets omit famous outcome labels where practical but pretrained historical memory may still leak. Any suspicious outcome-shaped specificity is retained as evidence.

cases.cutoff: 1973, after the relational proposal but before System R/SQL/cost-based optimization were validated

packet.pressure: Organizations need to ask changing questions over large shared data, but current programs navigate physical record links and indexes directly. A new relational proposal claims applications should specify what data they want rather than storage paths, but critics doubt practical performance.
availableEvidence: Hierarchical/network database systems are operational and can be fast for known paths.
A formal relational model has been published and promises data independence.
Disk/storage costs remain significant and query execution may require expensive joins/scans.
High-level query languages and industrial relational prototypes are not yet proven at scale.
Application programmers currently encode many physical access decisions manually.
liveRoutes: continue optimizing navigational databases and expose physical access paths
build a bounded relational prototype and benchmark representative queries against navigational baselines
adopt the relational model organization-wide immediately without a systems prototype
keep relational algebra as a research notation but preserve navigational execution interfaces
prototype several physical execution strategies under a declarative interface and measure their costs
constraints: existing production data cannot be risked
query workload must include both selective and multi-relation questions
the abstraction is useful only if a physical execution system can make it competitive

cases.hiddenOutcome: System R and related prototypes showed relational operation was feasible; SQL and cost-based optimization made declarative queries practical by selecting physical plans beneath the abstraction, followed by commercial RDBMS diffusion.

cases.cutoff: 1982, as European GSM coordination begins before a digital pan-European cellular system is deployed

packet.pressure: Several countries are building cellular service, but national/region-specific analog systems use different spectrum, signaling and equipment. Mobile users and suppliers face fragmented markets and limited roaming.
availableEvidence: Analog cellular architectures such as NMT and AMPS demonstrate that cellular mobile service is technically feasible.
NMT shows that multi-country roaming is possible when neighboring countries coordinate one system.
Digital radio/switching promises capacity, security and service advantages but is not yet a proven continent-scale cellular platform.
European governments control different spectrum allocations and procurement choices.
A larger common market could support more handset/network suppliers, but agreeing on interfaces may delay deployment or constrain local optimization.
liveRoutes: let each country choose its locally preferred cellular design
extend one existing analog regional standard across Europe
freeze a common pan-European digital architecture and interfaces before mass deployment
standardize only roaming/billing gateways while leaving radio systems incompatible
coordinate spectrum and a minimum interoperable interface while allowing bounded implementation competition
constraints: equipment vendors need enough market scale to invest
technology and spectrum decisions may lock in for years

cases.hiddenOutcome: GSM coordination standardized a digital cellular architecture and interfaces, created interoperable roaming and a large multi-vendor market, and spread globally alongside other standards rather than eliminating all alternatives.

cases.cutoff: 1980, after high-energy intercalation cells and a higher-voltage oxide cathode are known but before the later safe commercial lithium-ion architecture

packet.pressure: Portable devices and energy applications want a rechargeable battery much lighter than lead-acid/NiCd. Lithium/intercalation cells offer high voltage and energy, but repeated charging of metallic lithium can form irregular deposits and dangerous internal shorts.
availableEvidence: A rechargeable lithium-metal/TiS2 intercalation cell has demonstrated high energy.
Repeated cycling of metallic lithium can create whisker/dendrite growth and fire risk.
A higher-voltage layered metal-oxide cathode has been demonstrated.
Commercial rechargeable cells must survive many cycles, abuse and manufacturing variability.
Alternative rechargeable chemistries are safer but have lower energy density.
liveRoutes: continue metallic-lithium cells and focus on suppressing dendrites
pair the higher-voltage oxide cathode with metallic lithium and accept stronger containment
search for a reversible non-metallic host anode that stores lithium without plating bulk metal
abandon lithium rechargeability and optimize nickel-based cells
build small comparative cycling/abuse experiments before committing to a complete cell architecture
constraints: safety failures can destroy commercial viability
cycle life and retained capacity matter as much as first-cycle energy
electrolyte/separator compatibility may dominate cell behavior
portable-electronics demand rewards light weight but not catastrophic failure

cases.hiddenOutcome: Goodenough-type oxide cathodes plus Yoshino’s carbonaceous host anode removed metallic lithium from the charged cell architecture; commercial lithium-ion then achieved useful energy with repeatable cycling and improved safety.

cases.cutoff: 1984, a decade after the CFC ozone hypothesis but before the Antarctic ozone-hole publication

packet.pressure: Stable CFCs are valuable industrial chemicals, but atmospheric chemistry suggests long-lived molecules could reach the stratosphere, release chlorine and reduce protective ozone. The predicted effect is global, delayed and difficult to validate directly.
availableEvidence: A published chemical mechanism links CFC photolysis to catalytic ozone destruction.
CFC use is large and growing in aerosols, refrigeration and industrial processes.
Some national aerosol restrictions already exist, but industrial uses remain broad.
Long-term ground and satellite ozone measurements exist with calibration/coverage limits.
No dramatic continent-scale ozone-loss observation is yet established publicly.
Substitute technologies exist for some uses but not all, and international controls impose uneven costs.
liveRoutes: wait for an unmistakable global ozone-loss signal before further control
expand long-term measurements, instrument cross-checks and atmospheric chemistry while preserving reversible national controls
negotiate an international cooperation/monitoring framework before committing to quantitative production cuts
impose immediate worldwide elimination using current substitute technology
set staged controls with explicit revision points tied to independent observations and substitute availability
constraints: industry transition costs differ by application/country
irreversible ozone harm could make delayed evidence expensive

cases.hiddenOutcome: British Antarctic Survey measurements revealed the ozone hole in 1985, follow-up evidence strengthened the chlorine mechanism, and the Vienna/Montreal regime imposed staged controls that were repeatedly tightened as evidence and substitutes improved.
